segments.en: Early morning on the shore of Lake Victoria. Fishing boats slide out across the still water, a kingfisher dives, and on the roadside someone is already frying the first rolex of the day.
A rolex, by the way, is not a watch. It is a chapati rolled around a fried egg with tomato and onion, a name that comes from rolled eggs said quickly. It is Uganda's favourite street snack.
Uganda sits right on the equator in East Africa, yet much of it is high and green, with a mild climate. Rain falls often, and the land is so fertile that it has been called the Pearl of Africa.
Near the town of Jinja, the River Nile begins its long journey north, flowing out of Lake Victoria. Rafters come to ride its roaring rapids, while others simply watch the water rush past.
In the southwest, misty forests cover the hills. Here, in the Bwindi Impenetrable Forest, families of mountain gorillas live among the vines, and seeing one up close is a quiet, unforgettable moment.
Along the border with Congo rise the Rwenzori Mountains, sometimes called the Mountains of the Moon. Their highest peaks hold snow and glaciers, even so close to the equator.

Kampala, the capital, is built across green hills. It is lively and loud, full of boda bodas, the motorbike taxis that weave through traffic, and markets heaped with pineapples, avocados and jackfruit.

Uganda is home to many peoples and more than forty languages. English and Swahili are official, and Luganda is widely heard around Kampala. A friendly greeting in Luganda is oli otya, meaning how are you.
Greetings matter here. People take time to ask about your family and your journey, and in some communities it is polite to kneel slightly when greeting an elder.
Bananas are central to daily life. Green cooking bananas are steamed in their leaves and mashed into matooke, often served with groundnut sauce, beans or stew.
Traditional dress is proud and graceful. Women may wear the gomesi, a long dress with puffed shoulders and a sash, while men wear the kanzu, a long white robe.
Music and dance fill celebrations, with drums of every size, and Ugandan runners have become heroes at world championships and the Olympic Games.
So wave goodbye to the gorillas and follow the hills south, where the land of a thousand hills, Rwanda, is ready to welcome you.
